profile.profile: A solo dance is performed by an individual dancing alone, contrasting with couple or group choreography. Soloists often emerge as advanced members of a dance school after six to seven years of training. In traditions like Comparsas, soloists strut at the edges of streets while male dancers spin large lantern-like artifacts on poles. Across these contexts, solo dance functions as a direct expression of emotion.
profile.profile_long:
A solo dance is defined as a dance done by an individual dancing alone, as opposed to couples dancing together or groups dancing simultaneously in a coordinated manner. Solo dancers are usually the best dancers in a group or dance school, typically starting after about 6 to 7 years of dance or sooner. Most soloists are company kids from their dance school and participate in more than one dance.

In Comparsas, various soloists strut in front and usually dance at the edges of the street so that the viewing public can appreciate their moves. Most male soloists carry a large lantern-like artifact on a large pole, resting on an oily pouch, which they spin at will. Ultimately, dance serves as a way to express emotions. Related styles and traditions noted alongside solo dance include Sean-nós dance, Irish dance, step dance, and African-American stepping.
